title: A phase transition in monetary function explains expansion without inflation
summary: Ran Huang proposes that monetary function is 'phase-dependent,' meaning newly issued base money occupies distinct functional compartments with different coupling to prices. The paper introduces φ=RB/MB (reserve-share fraction) as an order parameter and, using Japan's data (1971-2026), identifies a compositional phase transition after 2013 from cash-dominated to reserve-dominated regime. Unexpected base-growth shocks are absorbed as reserve balances, strongly attenuating core CPI inflation response which can even reverse sign.
key_points: Order parameter φ = RB/MB (reserve-share fraction of monetary base) operationalizes the phase concept
Japan's data shows phase transition after 2013 from cash-dominated to reserve-dominated monetary regime
Phase transition is quantitatively captured using a Landau-type order-parameter framework
Unexpected base expansions are absorbed primarily as reserve balances, not entering consumption-goods transaction sector
Core CPI inflation response to monetary shocks is strongly attenuated and can reverse sign in reserve-dominated regime
Incremental money accumulation location (reservoir vs circulation) determines inflation outcome, not total supply
Paper defines function-specific efficiencies for reservation absorption and CPI transmission
why_it_matters: This research challenges the simplistic 'money supply drives inflation' view that underpins many monetary policy frameworks. For central banks considering QE or monetary expansion, the paper suggests that whether new money becomes reserves versus circulating in the economy determines inflationary impact. This has implications for how policy makers interpret balance sheet expansion and its transmission to price stability.
macro_context: The paper provides an analytical framework for understanding why Japanese monetary expansion post-2013 (Abenomics/QQE era) did not produce significant inflation. It suggests the reserve-dominated phase absorbed expansionary shocks in reserve balances rather than transmitting them to consumer prices. This challenges conventional monetary theory and has implications for evaluating QE programs globally.
